## Case study: how does a bike-share navigate speedy success?

Cyclistic, a bike-share company in Chicago, wants to grow annual memberships, since its stakeholders believe the company's future depends on them. The goal is a marketing strategy that converts casual riders into annual members. This report looks at how the two groups use the bikes differently, using all of 2020's trip data.

### Business task

1. How do annual members and casual riders use Cyclistic bikes differently?
2. Why would casual riders buy annual memberships?
3. How can Cyclistic use digital media to influence casual riders to become members?

This analysis answers question 1 with data and uses it to suggest directions for 2 and 3.

### Data source

Trip data comes from Motivate International Inc., which operates Chicago's Divvy bike-share service. The data is public [here](https://divvy-tripdata.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html) under this [license](https://www.divvybikes.com/data-license-agreement). Download the 2020 files (the Q1 file plus the April–December monthly files) into a `data/` folder next to this document.

## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
```

## Loading the data

All twelve files share the same columns, but `start_station_id` and `end_station_id` change type partway through the year, which makes `bind_rows()` fail. Reading every column as text first, then converting, avoids that.

```{r}
files <- c(
  "data/Divvy_Trips_2020_Q1.csv",
  sprintf("data/2020%02d-divvy-tripdata.csv", 4:12)
)

trips_raw <- files |>
  map(\(f) read_csv(f, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))) |>
  bind_rows()

glimpse(trips_raw)
```

## Cleaning

```{r}
trips <- trips_raw |>
  mutate(
    started_at  = ymd_hms(started_at),
    ended_at    = ymd_hms(ended_at),
    ride_min    = as.numeric(difftime(ended_at, started_at, units = "mins")),
    month       = month(started_at, label = TRUE),
    day_of_week = wday(started_at, label = TRUE, week_start = 1),
    weekend     = day_of_week %in% c("Sat", "Sun")
  )

n_before <- nrow(trips)

trips <- trips |>
  filter(
    !is.na(started_at), !is.na(ended_at), !is.na(member_casual),
    ride_min > 1,                                         # under a minute: false start or redock
    is.na(start_station_name) | start_station_name != "HQ QR"  # Divvy test/maintenance station
  )

n_after <- nrow(trips)
```

I removed `r format(n_before - n_after, big.mark = ",")` of `r format(n_before, big.mark = ",")` rows (`r round(100 * (n_before - n_after) / n_before, 1)`%): rides with missing timestamps or rider type, rides of one minute or less, and rides starting at Divvy's HQ test station. I kept rides with a missing station name, because those are mostly electric bikes parked away from a dock and dropping them would bias the sample.

A few rides last for days, which looks like bikes that weren't docked properly. Instead of dropping them, I report medians alongside means so a handful of outliers don't drive the conclusions.

```{r}
trips |>
  summarise(
    max_hours   = max(ride_min) / 60,
    p99_minutes = quantile(ride_min, 0.99),
    median_min  = median(ride_min)
  )
```

## How members and casual riders differ

### How many rides each group takes

```{r}
rides_by_group <- trips |>
  count(member_casual) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

rides_by_group
```

```{r}
ggplot(rides_by_group, aes(member_casual, n, fill = member_casual)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casual = "#FF9912", member = "#03A89E")) +
  labs(title = "Total rides in 2020", x = NULL, y = "Rides")
```

### When they ride

```{r}
by_day <- trips |>
  count(member_casual, day_of_week)

ggplot(by_day, aes(day_of_week, n, fill = member_casual)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casual = "#FF9912", member = "#03A89E")) +
  labs(title = "Rides by day of week", x = NULL, y = "Rides", fill = NULL)
```

```{r}
weekend_share <- trips |>
  group_by(member_casual) |>
  summarise(weekend_share = mean(weekend))

weekend_share
```

```{r}
by_month <- trips |>
  count(member_casual, month)

ggplot(by_month, aes(month, n, colour = member_casual, group = member_casual)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(casual = "#FF9912", member = "#03A89E")) +
  labs(title = "Rides per month", x = NULL, y = "Rides", colour = NULL)
```

### How long they ride

```{r}
duration_summary <- trips |>
  group_by(member_casual) |>
  summarise(
    median_min = median(ride_min),
    mean_min   = mean(ride_min),
    total_hours = sum(ride_min) / 60
  )

duration_summary
```

```{r}
ggplot(trips, aes(member_casual, ride_min, fill = member_casual)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 90)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(casual = "#FF9912", member = "#03A89E")) +
  labs(title = "Ride length (outliers hidden, axis capped at 90 min)",
       x = NULL, y = "Minutes")
```

## Findings

```{r}
#| include: false
ws  <- deframe(weekend_share)
med <- deframe(select(duration_summary, member_casual, median_min))
pct <- \(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
```

- **Weekends vs weekdays.** `r pct(ws["casual"])` of casual rides happen on weekends, compared with `r pct(ws["member"])` of member rides. Members ride through the work week; casual riders cluster on Saturdays and Sundays.
- **Ride length.** The median casual ride is `r round(med["casual"])` minutes, against `r round(med["member"])` minutes for members. Casual riders use the bikes for longer, leisure-style trips; members make shorter, regular trips.
- **Seasonality.** Both groups peak in summer, but the monthly chart shows how much more seasonal casual riding is.

*(Check each line against the rendered numbers and charts before sharing.)*

## Recommendations

1. **Target casual riders where and when they already ride.** Run membership promotions on weekends and in late spring, before the summer peak, at the stations casual riders use most. A next step would be ranking start stations by casual share.
2. **Sell the membership on cost per ride for long trips.** Casual riders take longer rides, so pricing that shows what a member would have saved on their own recent rides speaks directly to how they use the service.
3. **Use digital channels for the weekend/leisure crowd.** App notifications and social ads timed for Friday afternoons and spring weekends, with a seasonal or weekend-focused membership tier to test against the standard annual plan.

## Limitations

- The data has no rider IDs, so I can't tell how many distinct people are behind the casual rides, or whether the same people ride repeatedly.
- 2020 was heavily affected by COVID-19, so commuting patterns, and the gap between members and casual riders, may not carry over to normal years.
